description: General knowledge. RULES are background facts that serve as premises; each sits on the card(s) in attaches_to and appears with them (they appear in constraints); 'stated_in' is where the story finally says them, usually only in Holmes's explanation. GLOSSES are background for a modern reader: what an 1892 reader would simply have known. Glosses marked editorial were written for this game, not taken from the story. Editorial background facts (editorial: true) are true but play no part in the solution; they keep the clue-relevant facts from standing out.

rules.text: Powdered opium is not tasteless. Mixed into an ordinary dish the eater would notice it and probably eat no more.
source:
Powdered opium
      is by no means tasteless
rules.relevant_from: an appreciable quantity of powdered opium

rules.text: Strong spices such as curry hide other tastes in a dish.
source:
A
      curry was exactly the medium which would disguise this taste

rules.text: Holmes distrusts coincidence: when exactly the thing a plan needed turns up by chance, he asks who arranged it.
source:
it is surely too monstrous a coincidence to suppose
      that he happened to come along with powdered opium upon the very
      night when a dish happened to be served
unless: the drugger brought the drug on the chance of some dish or drink that would hide it

rules.text: In a small household with one maid, it is the master or the mistress who decides what is cooked for supper.
source:
By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson,
      have caused curry to be served in the trainer’s family that
      night
unless: the cook or maid chose the dish herself

rules.text: What a house will have for supper is known beforehand only to the people of its own establishment.
source:
By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson,
      have caused curry to be served in the trainer’s family that
      night
unless: someone of the house let it out

rules.text: A man who brings a drug that must be hidden, on the one night a dish that hides it is served, arranged for that dish: he is one of those who decide what the house eats.
source:
By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson,
      have caused curry to be served in the trainer’s family that
      night
unless: he learned the menu from someone in the house

rules.text: When a drug is found in one person's portion and others ate the same dish without harm, the drug was put into that portion, not into the dish.
source:
The opium was added after the dish
      was set aside for the stable-boy, for the others had the same for
      supper with no ill effects

rules.text: A stable dog is kept to give the alarm: it barks at strangers, not at the people it knows.
source:
Obviously the midnight visitor was some one
      whom the dog knew well
unless: the dog was asleep, drugged, muzzled or shut away
the dog did bark and nobody heard

rules.text: A stable dog knows well the people of its own establishment; anyone else is a stranger to it.
source:
Obviously the midnight visitor was some one
      whom the dog knew well
unless: a frequent caller the dog has come to know

rules.text: A locked door is opened again with its key, or from inside; forcing it leaves marks.
source:
The window, I may add, was
      not large enough for a man to get through
rules.relevant_from: The boy locked the door before he left it

rules.text: Opium is given as a sleeping draught. A man meant to stay awake on guard is not secretly given a sleeping draught for any honest reason.
source:
For a dishonest one, obviously,
      or why should he drug his own stable-boy?
rules.relevant_from: an appreciable quantity of powdered opium

rules.text: Surgeons use a cataract knife — a long, narrow, very delicate blade — for the finest operations; it would be a useless weapon.
source:
a knife which certainly
      no sane man would choose for a weapon

rules.text: A slight nick to the tendons of a horse's ham, made under the skin, leaves no mark; the horse goes a little lame, which is blamed on a strain or rheumatism.
source:
it is possible to make a slight
      nick upon the tendons of a horse’s ham

rules.text: An owner or trainer can make money by betting, through agents, that his own horse will lose — and then seeing that it does.
source:
trainers have
      made sure of great sums of money by laying against their own
      horses, through agents, and then preventing them from winning by
      fraud
rules.relevant_from: the betting being three to one on him

rules.text: A spirited horse that is hurt usually plunges and squeals, loudly enough to wake people sleeping close by.
source:
So spirited a creature would have
      certainly roused the soundest of sleepers when it felt the prick
      of the knife

rules.text: A light down in a deep hollow cannot be seen from houses some way off across the surrounding ground.
source: a hollow where his light would be invisible
rules.relevant_from: a bowl-shaped depression in the moor

rules.text: A horse startled from behind — by a sudden glare, say — lashes out with its hind feet; a shod hoof can kill a man.
source:
the creature frightened at the sudden glare,
      and with the strange instinct of animals feeling that some
      mischief was intended, had lashed out

rules.text: On a night with no wind a coat cannot be blown onto a bush: if it hangs there, someone put it there.
source:
In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush,
      but placed there
rules.relevant_from: overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush

rules.text: A knife bloody to the handle in a fighting man's hand usually means it wounded someone.
source:
the
      state of Straker’s knife would show that one at least of his
      assailants must bear his mark upon him
rules.relevant_from: clotted with blood up to the handle

rules.text: After a heavy blow to the head a man may struggle convulsively, and can wound himself with whatever he is holding.
source:
caused by his own knife in the convulsive
      struggles which follow any brain injury

rules.text: A man does not carry other people's bills about in his pockets; he has enough to do settling his own.
source:
men do not
      carry other people’s bills about in their pockets
rules.relevant_from: a milliner’s account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen
unless: he was carrying it for someone else, or had picked it up

rules.text: A servant's wages, however liberal, do not run to the most fashionable dresses.
source:
one can hardly expect that they can
      buy twenty-guinea walking dresses for their ladies
rules.relevant_from: Twenty-two guineas is rather heavy for a single costume

rules.text: A careful man about to do a delicate piece of work for the first time practises it first on something that does not matter.
source:
so astute a man as Straker would not undertake this delicate
      tendon-nicking without a little practice

rules.text: A horse is a gregarious creature: loose, it makes for its own stable or the nearest other one rather than staying alone on open moor.
source: The horse is a very gregarious creature

rules.text: (A prejudice of the period.) Gypsies were said to clear out at the first sign of trouble to avoid the police.
source:
These people always clear out when
      they hear of trouble

rules.text: A famous racehorse cannot be sold or kept hidden for long without someone recognising it.
source: They could not hope to sell such a horse
rules.relevant_from: the most remarkable horse in England

rules.text: Hard, dry moorland keeps no tracks; ground that was wet keeps them for days.
source:
If our supposition is
      correct, then the horse must have crossed that, and there is the
      point where we should look for his tracks

rules.text: Holmes's method: a boot of an unusual shape that fits a print exactly identifies the wearer.
source:
his own boots exactly
      corresponded to them
rules.relevant_from: one of the boots which Straker wore

rules.text: Dishonest dealers ('horse-fakers') can hide a horse's white markings with dye, which spirits of wine will wash off.
source: Oh, an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge.
rules.relevant_from: the betting being three to one on him

rules.text: Horses are told apart by their markings — a white face, a white or mottled leg — unless the markings have been hidden.
source: A child would know Silver Blaze

rules.text: When the odds on a horse suddenly shorten, someone with knowledge is backing it.
source: Somebody knows something, that is clear.
rules.relevant_from: the betting being three to one on him

rules.text: A horse in a race carries its owner's registered colours, and the board shows which numbers are running.
source:
My colours have not
      passed

rules.text: A horse does not bridle itself or open a stable door: someone must do it.
source:
His bridle is missing, so that Simpson
      must have put this on
rules.relevant_from: One of these lads sat up each night in the stable

rules.text: Clothes still wet the next day say their wearer was out in the rain.
source:
His wet clothing showed that he had
      been out in the storm of the night before

rules.text: Telegraph posts along a railway are set at a regular spacing, so counting them against a watch gives a train's speed.
source:
the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty
      yards apart
rules.relevant_from: the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart

rules.text: Flat-race horses run from two years old; a racehorse's age is counted from 1 January.
rules.relevant_from: He is now in his fifth year

rules.text: Jockeys must carry the weight given to their horse; lead is added under the saddle to make it up.
Trainers keep their horses' form secret, and touts try to watch them at exercise.
The odds on a favourite lengthen when there is doubt that it will run.
rules.relevant_from: the betting being three to one on him

rules.text: Horses are measured in hands of four inches.
A horse's shoes are nailed on and renewed every few weeks; a shoe that comes off is 'cast'.
rules.relevant_from: a cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze

rules.text: A horse is described by its colour (bay, chestnut, grey) and its white markings (star, blaze, stocking).
Horses can doze standing up.
A racehorse is led by its bridle; a halter is enough to tie it up.
Racehorses are fed oats, hay and chopped straw ('chaff'), and watered several times a day.
Stable-lads live in, often sleeping in a loft above the stable.
rules.relevant_from: the others slept in the loft

rules.text: Saddles, bridles and harness are kept in the harness-room.
rules.relevant_from: the chaff-cutting loft above the harness-room

rules.text: The horses are exercised in the morning, on the gallops.
rules.relevant_from: taken out the horse for early exercise

rules.text: In a small household the maid rises first, to light the fires and the kitchen range.
Servants are paid monthly or quarterly, with their board and lodging.
Tradesmen send their accounts to the house, usually at each quarter-day.
rules.relevant_from: a milliner’s account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen

rules.text: A careful man keeps his receipted bills.
Laudanum — opium dissolved in alcohol — is given for pain, coughs and sleeplessness.
rules.relevant_from: an appreciable quantity of powdered opium

rules.text: A blow that breaks the skull usually leaves a man senseless at once.
Surgical instruments are made by specialist cutlers, many of them in London.
A doctor carries his instruments in a case, their edges guarded.
Holmes holds that it is a capital mistake to theorise before one has the data.
Holmes elsewhere: when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.
Holmes sifts 'the framework of fact' from 'the embellishments of theorists and reporters'.
Dartmoor is grazed by ponies, sheep and cattle.
Moorland weather changes fast; mist can come down in minutes.
Furze (gorse) grows thickly on the moor.
rules.relevant_from: overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush

rules.text: Bracken turns bronze in the autumn.

glosses.text: A fictional race. 'Wessex' is the old name for south-west England that Thomas Hardy had made popular.

Odds of 'three to one on' mean you stake £3 to win £1: the horse is expected to win. Odds 'against' mean the opposite: at 'ten to one' you stake £1 to win £10. When more money is placed on a horse, its odds 'shorten'.
glosses.after: the betting being three to one on him

glosses.text: To 'lay' a horse is to bet, as a bookmaker does, that it will not win.
glosses.after: registered by him against the favourite

glosses.text: Taking bets from others at agreed odds; a bookmaker 'makes a book' and pays out only on the horses that win.
A man who spies on racing stables for information to sell or bet on. Stable-lads were warned against them and often bribed by them.
Reliable inside information about a horse's chances.

glosses.term: 'At the weights … give the other a hundred yards in five furlongs'
glosses.text: In a handicap race each horse carries a set weight to even out the field. The question is whether Bayard, with the weight he has been given, is really the faster horse. A furlong is an eighth of a mile (about 200 m).

The owner owns the horses; the trainer runs the training stable and its staff for him; the jockey rides in races; stable-lads feed, groom, exercise and guard the horses. A trainer is a paid servant of the owner.
Jockeys are weighed before a race; Straker grew too heavy to ride, so he became a trainer.
A real and very famous racehorse (foaled 1875), twice winner of the Ascot Gold Cup. To be 'of the Isonomy stock' is to come from a champion's bloodline.
Races were started by a man dropping a flag.
Withdrawn from a race before it is run.
Each owner registers a pattern of cap and jacket ('silks') that his jockeys wear, so spectators can tell the horses apart.

glosses.term: '50 sovs each h ft with 1000 sovs added'
glosses.text: Each owner pays a stake of 50 sovereigns to enter, of which half is forfeit ('h ft') if the horse is withdrawn; the course adds 1,000 sovereigns to the prize. Open to four- and five-year-olds.
The bookmakers at a racecourse, shouting the odds they offer.
A dishonest dealer who disguises horses — dyeing coats, hiding markings and blemishes — to pass one horse off as another.
A horse with a reddish-brown body and black mane, tail and lower legs.
The horse's right front leg ('near' is the left side, the side you lead from).
The back of the hind leg above the hock, where the tendons run. A tendon injury there makes a horse lame.
A short wax match, struck on the box; what a man carried to light his pipe or cigar.
A cheap candle made of animal fat.
A sweetened pipe tobacco.
A pipe of briar root, the usual material.
£1 = 20 shillings. A sovereign is a £1 gold coin. A guinea is £1 1s, the unit for fashionable goods and fees. A half-crown is 2s 6d. A maid-of-all-work might earn £12–£20 a year.
A maker and seller of women's hats and, in the West End, dresses and trimmings. Bond Street was the most fashionable shopping street in London.
A woman's outfit for wearing out of doors. A very fashionable one could cost more than a maid earned in a year.
Keeping a mistress in a separate household, often under a false name — a serious scandal for a married servant.
Bills marked as paid.
A surgeon's knife with a long, narrow, very sharp blade, made for cutting into the eye to remove a cataract. It does not fold.
A common Victorian drug, sold by chemists (after the Pharmacy Act of 1868, only by registered chemists) as a painkiller and sleeping draught; a large dose stupefies.
Curry was an everyday English dish by the 1890s, often a way to use up cold mutton.
A household with one servant did its own cooking with her help; the mistress (or master) decided the meals.
A loft where hay and straw are chopped into 'chaff' for feed; the lads sleep there, above the harness-room where saddles and bridles are kept.
A walking stick made of a small palm from Penang, with a heavy knob; the joke in the name is that it 'settles disputes'.
A rubberised waterproof overcoat.
A man's neckcloth of silk or linen, worn tied at the throat.
Coverings of cloth or leather over the shoe and ankle, worn for walking in mud.
Gorse: a spiny evergreen shrub common on moorland.
A high, wild moorland in Devon, with granite tors, bogs, scattered farms and old tin-mine workings.
Romani travellers, who camped on moors and commons. Writing of the period often repeats the prejudice that they are thieves who flee the police.
Messages sent by telegraph and delivered by hand, often within hours; to 'wire' someone is to telegraph them.
A coroner's public inquiry into a sudden death, often held in a house or inn near where the body lies.
A barrister arguing a case in court.
Binoculars.
Strong alcohol, used as a solvent: it would dissolve many dyes.
Horse-drawn carriages: a landau has a folding top; a drag is a private coach, used at races as a grandstand on wheels.
A luxurious railway carriage with armchairs.
Real London dailies, the Daily Telegraph and the Daily Chronicle; 'fresh editions' came out through the day.
Marks of a fashionable gentleman: a monocle, a long formal coat, and trimmed whiskers on the cheeks.
